title: Part 2, Chapter 73
paragraphs: The omens Don Quixote encountered as he entered his own village, together with other incidents that adorn and brighten this great history

At the edge of the village, Cide Hamete tells us, Don Quixote came upon two boys arguing on the village threshing-floor, and one of them said to the other, “Don't wear yourself out, Periquillo; you'll never lay eyes on it again as long as you live.”
Don Quixote caught the words and turned to Sancho. “Did you notice, my friend, what that boy just said? ‘You'll never lay eyes on it again as long as you live.’”
“Well,” said Sancho, “what difference does it make that the boy said it?”
“What!” said Don Quixote. “Can't you see that if you apply those words to the object of my longing, they mean I am never to see Dulcinea again?”

Sancho was about to reply when something distracted him: a hare came tearing across the plain with a pack of greyhounds and huntsmen after it. Terrified, the animal bolted for cover and tried to hide itself under Dapple. Sancho scooped it up alive and held it out to Don Quixote, who was muttering, “_Malum signum, malum signum!_ A hare runs, greyhounds give chase, and Dulcinea does not appear.”

“Your worship is a strange one,” said Sancho. “Suppose we grant that this hare is Dulcinea, and that the greyhounds chasing her are the wicked enchanters who turned her into a peasant girl. She runs, I catch her and place her in your worship's hands, and you hold her in your arms and pet her — where is the bad sign in that? What sort of evil omen can anyone find here?”

The two quarrelling boys wandered over to look at the hare, and Sancho asked one of them what the fight had been about. The answer came from the one who had said “You'll never see it again as long as you live”: he had taken a cage full of crickets from the other boy and had no intention of returning it for the rest of his days. Sancho fished four cuartos out of his pocket, paid the boy for the cage, and placed it in Don Quixote's hands, saying, “There, señor! There are your omens, smashed and done away with; and to my mind — fool though I am — they have no more bearing on our affairs than last year's clouds. If I remember rightly, I've heard the curate of our village say that it ill becomes Christians or people of sense to pay attention to such nonsense; and indeed your worship told me the very same thing a while back — that any Christian who took notice of omens was a fool. So there's no point wasting words on it; let's press on and get into the village.”

The huntsmen rode up and asked for their hare, and Don Quixote handed it over. They continued on, and on the green at the entrance of the town they ran into the curate and the bachelor Samson Carrasco, occupied with their breviaries. It should be said that Sancho had draped over Dapple, by way of a pack-cloth, on top of the bundle of armour, the buckram robe painted with flames that had been put on him at the duke's castle the night Altisidora came back from the dead. He had also fitted the mitre onto Dapple's head — the strangest costume and transformation any donkey in the world has ever undergone. Both the curate and the bachelor recognised them at once and came toward them with arms outstretched. Don Quixote dismounted and embraced them warmly; and the village boys, who are lynxes from whom nothing is hidden, spotted the donkey's mitre and came running to look, shouting to one another, “Come and see, boys! Sancho Panza's donkey is decked out finer than Mingo, and Don Quixote's nag is skinnier than ever!”

And so at last, with the boys leaping about them and the curate and the bachelor at their side, they made their entry into the town and headed for Don Quixote's house, where they found the housekeeper and his niece waiting at the door, the news of his arrival having already reached them. Word had also been carried to Teresa Panza, Sancho's wife, and she — hair flying loose, half dressed, dragging her daughter Sanchica along by the hand — ran out to meet her husband. But when she saw him arriving in nothing like the style she imagined a governor should travel in, she said to him, “What's this, husband, coming home like this? You look to me as if you'd tramped the whole way on sore feet — more like a shiftless vagabond than a governor.”

“Quiet, Teresa,” said Sancho. “Often enough ‘where you find the pegs there's no bacon hanging on them.’ Let's go inside the house, and there you'll hear things to astonish you. I'm bringing money, which is what counts, and I earned it by my own labour without doing wrong to a soul.”
“Just you bring the money, my good husband,” said Teresa, “and never mind whether it came this way or that; however you came by it, you won't have invented any new custom in the world.”

Sanchica hugged her father and asked whether he had brought her anything, for she had been watching for him the way one watches for the rains of May; and with her holding on to his belt on one side, and his wife taking his hand, while the girl led Dapple, they set off for their house — leaving Don Quixote in his own, in the care of his niece and housekeeper and in the company of the curate and the bachelor.

Don Quixote, paying no heed to time or occasion, immediately drew the bachelor and the curate aside in private. In a few words he told them of his defeat, and of the obligation he was now under not to leave his village for a year — a pledge he intended to honour to the letter, without straying from it by a hair's breadth, as befitted a knight-errant bound by scrupulous good faith and the laws of knight-errantry. He explained that he was thinking of becoming a shepherd for that year and amusing himself in the solitude of the fields, where he could give his loving thoughts free rein while practising the virtuous pastoral calling; and he begged them, if they were not too busy and no weightier business stood in the way, to agree to be his companions, for he would buy enough sheep to qualify them all as shepherds. The most important part of the whole scheme, he told them, was already settled: he had picked out names for them that fitted like a glove. The curate asked what they were. Don Quixote answered that he himself would be called the shepherd Quixotize, the bachelor the shepherd Carrascon, the curate the shepherd Curambro, and Sancho Panza the shepherd Pancino.

The two of them were dumbfounded by Don Quixote's latest madness; but rather than risk his slipping away from the village once more in pursuit of his chivalry, and trusting that over the course of the year he might be cured, they went along with his new scheme, applauded his crazy notion as a stroke of brilliance, and offered to join him in the life. “What's more,” said Samson Carrasco, “as everyone knows, I am a very celebrated poet, and I'll be turning out verses at every opportunity — pastoral, or courtly, or whatever comes into my head — to pass the time in those lonely places where we'll be wandering. But the most essential thing, gentlemen, is for each of us to choose the name of the shepherdess he intends to celebrate in his verses, and for us never to leave a tree, however hard the bark, without writing and carving her name into it, as is the habit and custom of lovesick shepherds.”

“Exactly right,” said Don Quixote, “although I myself am spared the trouble of inventing an imaginary shepherdess, since I have the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso — the glory of these brookbanks, the ornament of these meadows, the pillar of beauty, the cream of every grace, and, in short, a being to whom all praise is fitting, however extravagant it may be.”
“Quite true,” said the curate; “but the rest of us will have to hunt up obliging shepherdesses who will suit our purposes one way or another.”

“And if they fail us,” added Samson Carrasco, “we can borrow the names of the printed ones the world is stuffed with — Fílidas, Amarilises, Dianas, Fleridas, Galateas, Belisardas. Since they're sold in the marketplaces, we may fairly buy them and make them our own. If my lady — or rather my shepherdess — should happen to be named Ana, I'll sing her praises under the name Anarda; if Francisca, I'll call her Francenia; if Lucia, Lucinda; it all amounts to the same thing. And Sancho Panza, if he joins this brotherhood, can celebrate his wife Teresa Panza under the name Teresaina.”

Don Quixote laughed at the fitting of the name, and the curate heaped praise on his worthy and honourable resolution, offering once again to keep him company whenever he could spare time from his pressing duties. With that they said their goodbyes, urging and begging him to look after his health and to eat what was good for him.

As it happened, his niece and the housekeeper had overheard everything the three of them said, and the moment the visitors were gone the two women came in to Don Quixote. “What's all this, uncle?” said the niece. “Just when we were thinking you'd come home to stay and live a quiet, respectable life here, do you mean to tangle yourself up in new schemes and go playing ‘young shepherd coming hither, young shepherd going hence’? No indeed — ‘the straw is too hard now for making pipes.’”

“And how,” the housekeeper added, “is your worship going to stand the summer heat out in the fields, and the winter cold, and the howling of the wolves? You won't; that's a life and a trade for tough men, raised and hardened to such work almost from the cradle. If you have to choose between evils, better a knight-errant than a shepherd! Look, señor, take my advice — and I give it not on a full stomach of bread and wine but fasting, and with fifty years on my head — stay at home, see to your affairs, go often to confession, be generous to the poor, and let it be on my soul if any harm comes to you.”

“That's enough, my daughters,” said Don Quixote. “I know perfectly well where my duty lies. Help me to bed, for I'm not feeling well; and you may be certain that, knight-errant today or wandering shepherd tomorrow, I shall never stop looking after your interests, as you'll see in the end.” And the good women (for good they undoubtedly were), the housekeeper and the niece, helped him to bed, where they brought him something to eat and made him as comfortable as they could.
